questions.question: For $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$, how do the mean and variance compare?
options: variance is always greater than the mean
questions.explanation: For $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$, the mean is $np$ and the variance is $np(1-p)$; since $1-p\le1$, the variance never exceeds the mean.
questions.skill_detail: binomial variance does not exceed its mean
questions.source_support: Binomial variance $\le$ mean.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: The variance $np(1-p)$ is at most $np$, so it is not always greater than the mean.
Mean equals variance only when $p=0$; in general $np(1-p)\neq np$.
The variance is $np(1-p)$, which equals $np$ only in the degenerate case $p=0$.

questions.question: Doubling $n$ in $\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$ with $p$ fixed multiplies the variance by:
questions.explanation: The variance $np(1-p)$ is linear in $n$, so doubling $n$ (with $p$ fixed) doubles the variance.
questions.skill_detail: binomial variance is linear in n
questions.source_support: Variance $\propto n$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Halving would require the variance to fall, but it is linear in $n$, so it doubles.
A factor of $4$ would arise if the variance grew like $n^2$; here it is linear in $n$.
A factor of $1$ would mean no change, but doubling $n$ doubles the variance.

questions.question: What is the PMF formula for $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$?
questions.explanation: The binomial PMF is $P(X=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ for $k=0,\dots,n$.
questions.source_support: The definition gives $P(X=k)=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$.

$e^{-p}p^k/k!$ is the Poisson PMF, not the binomial.
